title: Protecting Yourself Day to Day
introduction: In this module, you will learn simple everyday habits to keep your bank details, passwords, payments and personal information safe.

sections.heading: Keeping your banking details safe
paragraphs: Your PIN, online banking password and one-time security codes protect your money. A one-time code is a short number your bank sends to confirm it is really you. Never share these with someone who contacts you unexpectedly, even if they say they are from your bank. To bank online, use your bank's official app or website.
tips: If someone asks you for a security code, end the conversation and contact your bank using the number on the back of your card.

sections.heading: Creating strong passwords
paragraphs: A strong password is long and hard to guess, such as three random words joined together. Use a different password for each important account, so one stolen password cannot unlock the rest. A password manager can create and remember them for you. Two-factor authentication adds an extra check when you sign in, such as a code sent to your phone.
tips: Turn on two-factor authentication for your email and banking if you can. It is sometimes called two-step verification.

sections.heading: Staying safe when shopping or paying online
paragraphs: When shopping online, type the shop's address yourself or use its official app, rather than following a payment link from an unexpected message. A padlock symbol, or your browser saying the connection is secure, means the connection is private. It does not prove that the seller is honest. Before you pay, check the amount and who you are paying.
tips: Check your bank statements or banking app regularly, and tell your bank straight away if you see a payment you do not recognise.

sections.heading: Protecting your personal information
paragraphs: Your address, date of birth and account details can be used to pretend to be you, so share them only when you need to. Be careful about posting personal details online. Install updates on your phone and computer when they are offered, because they often fix security problems. Lock your devices when you are not using them.
tips: If someone asks for your personal information unexpectedly, pause and check who they are using contact details you have found yourself.

quiz.question: Someone phones saying they are from your bank. They ask you to read out a security code that has just been sent to your phone. What should you do?
options: Read out the code, because the caller already knows your name.
Do not share the code, end the call and contact your bank using the number on the back of your card.
Send the code by text message instead of saying it aloud.
quiz.explanation: Security codes are only for you, and sharing one could let someone into your account. Ending the call and contacting your bank using a number you trust lets you check safely.

quiz.question: Which habit helps protect you when shopping or paying online?
options: Clicking a payment link in an unexpected text message to get a discount.
Trusting any website that shows a padlock symbol.
Checking the amount and who you are paying before you confirm a payment.
quiz.explanation: Checking the payment details helps you spot a wrong amount or an unfamiliar seller before you pay. A padlock only means the connection is private, not that the seller is genuine.
